subjects.displayTitle: Prayer for martyrs: remembrance, mercy, and those who remain
subjects.introduction: The loss of a life leaves both a memory and a living community in need of care. These prayers place those who suffered for their faith within an expansive hope of mercy, nearness, light, and continuing life, while also asking for patience and renewal for bereaved families. Their language carries the intensity of persecution and mourning; images of sacrifice and a desired cup of martyrdom belong to that devotional setting, rather than a general invitation to seek death or inflict suffering. Individual eulogies and prayers of visitation also preserve distinct people and occasions within the wider subject. The connected compilation on martyrdom brings grief itself into view, alongside hope for enduring spiritual fruit. Stephen’s final prayer in Acts provides a comparison centered on entrusting his spirit to Jesus and asking forgiveness for his killers [1]. Reading these texts together invites reflection on remembrance that deepens compassion and sustains the living.
subjects.arc: Begin with mercy and consolation, encounter particular lives and shared remembrance, and turn toward the care and service of those who remain.

Compare this joining of hope and forgiveness with the compilation’s prayers for mercy and continuing life. Acts presents the dying person’s prayer, whereas many selections here are prayers of remembrance or visitation spoken for others.

subjects.displayTitle: Prayer for prosperity: the good of this world and the next
subjects.introduction: What counts as a life made prosperous? These prayers make room for plainly material needs: a diminished livelihood, a troubled business, a family’s security, and relief from poverty. At the same time, they repeatedly widen the request toward what will benefit a person in every world, linking sustenance with faithfulness, spiritual independence, and service. The result is a richer inquiry than the size of one’s possessions alone can answer. The connected subject on wealth and poverty asks how attachment may obstruct this wider good, while prayers for cooperation turn resources toward the needs of others. Particular assurances addressed to individuals retain their own circumstances; the collection offers words of supplication rather than a formula guaranteeing financial outcomes. Qur’an 2:200–202 provides a close comparison by contrasting a request confined to worldly bounty with one that seeks good here and hereafter [1]. Prayer can thus become an education of desire as well as an expression of need.
subjects.arc: Begin with concrete hardship, widen the meaning of riches, and carry the prayer for provision toward family, community, and service.

Compare that widened horizon with the repeated petitions in this compilation. The Qur’anic setting retains its own ritual and theological context while offering a close connection between prayer, desire, and responsibility.

subjects.displayTitle: Preserving the writings: fidelity in human hands
subjects.introduction: A text can be treasured and still be copied inaccurately, misplaced, or lost. This compilation brings the practical labor of preservation into the heart of devotion: gather scattered writings, compare copies, correct errors, choose durable materials, protect originals, and share trustworthy texts. The passages reveal both urgency and patience, from the fear of failing to record words during revelation to the repeated checking of pages before circulation. Instructions about secrecy reflect particular dangers of confiscation and persecution; other selections call for dissemination and placement in libraries. The connected subjects of authentication, ordering, translation, and textual discrepancies help distinguish reverence for revelation from confidence in every human copy. Jeremiah’s account of a burned scroll and its renewed dictation offers a vivid comparison of a message surviving an attack on its material form [1]. The reader is invited to see accurate preservation as an active trust owed to both the words and their future readers.
subjects.arc: Begin with the vulnerability of transmission, follow careful copying and protection, and consider access, remembrance, and enduring meaning.

The additional prophetic words are part of Jeremiah’s narrative; they are distinct from a copyist altering an entrusted text on personal authority.

subjects.displayTitle: The mind’s power of discovery: bringing the hidden into view
subjects.introduction: An invention that reshapes daily life may begin with a relation no one has yet understood. These passages celebrate the mind’s capacity to move from observed signs toward hidden realities, to discover laws, and to give ideas a practical form. They also ask what makes discovery trustworthy: examine premises, attend to experience, and distinguish the reach of human investigation from claims about divine realities. The connected subjects of reason’s limits, concentration, scientific knowledge, and religion help keep intellectual confidence open to correction. Historical examples and comparisons with animals belong to the texts’ philosophical arguments and should be examined in that setting. Bacon offers a productive comparison by joining knowledge and effective action to observation, instruments, and respect for nature’s workings [1]. Read together, these perspectives invite a question of responsibility as well as ability: how can the gift of understanding become a disciplined search for truth and a source of benefit?
subjects.arc: Begin with discovery’s visible fruits, examine reasoning and observation, and explore the scope, limits, and purposes of understanding.

Bacon’s account here concerns inquiry and practical action; it does not establish the Bahá’í passages’ theological account of the human spirit.

subjects.displayTitle: Future revelation: an open horizon and a firm minimum
subjects.introduction: A revelation that affirms its own greatness can also prepare its followers to recognize revelation still to come. This compilation holds that openness together with an explicit safeguard: the full thousand-year minimum before a new claim to direct revelation. It repeatedly distinguishes that minimum from an appointed arrival date, and a particular dispensation from the much longer cycle within which further Manifestations may appear. The connected subjects of progressive revelation, false claims, and prophecy make discernment central. The sources need to be weighed as well as compared: provisional translations and reported sayings retain their status, and a report suggesting a conclusion before a thousand years conflicts with the explicit minimum. Matthew’s call to readiness without knowledge of the day or hour offers a comparison, while providing no equivalent thousand-year rule [1]. The inquiry therefore concerns both patient fidelity and the humility needed to leave future divine action open.
subjects.arc: Begin with the promise of further revelation, establish the minimum interval, distinguish dispensation and cycle, and return to recognition and responsibility.

subjects.displayTitle: The influence of one soul: faith shared through a life
subjects.introduction: A single act of kindness, a sustained friendship, or a patient conversation may set in motion effects that its author never sees. These selections approach the influence of one person through images of seeds, lamps, sparks, fruitful trees, and a life-giving chain of relationships. Their confidence rests on sincerity, preparation, and divine assistance, while the connected subjects of teaching methods and the power of faith direct attention toward how that influence is exercised. Historical reports and sweeping examples retain their particular voices; their purpose here is to prompt inquiry into spiritual capacity, rather than make social transformation the achievement of an isolated hero. The later guidance brings this hope into close association, loving service, answers to questions, and shared action. In John’s Gospel, a woman’s testimony invites others to encounter Jesus, and they eventually speak from their own hearing [1]. The comparison opens a discussion of influence that awakens another person’s understanding and participation.
subjects.arc: Begin with the possible reach of a single deed, examine preparation and selflessness, and follow personal relationships into shared spiritual life.

references.note: A woman’s testimony brings people from her city to Jesus; they later say that their belief rests on hearing him for themselves. Between these events, Jesus speaks of sowing and reaping in work shared across people. Compare this pattern with the compilation’s chain of influence and its emphasis on personal relationships. John’s account concerns recognition of Jesus as the Christ; it offers a narrative comparison rather than a universal formula for teaching.
